# Base image: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS for a stable, well-supported environment
FROM ubuntu:22.04

# Set non-interactive frontend for package installations to prevent prompts
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Configure Open MPI for containerized environments like Kubernetes
# This allows running MPI processes as the root user inside the container
ENV OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT=1
ENV OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT_CONFIRM=1

# Install build dependencies, MPI, LAMMPS prerequisites, and required certificates
# Added python3 to satisfy the LAMMPS CMake build system requirement
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential \
    cmake \
    git \
    python3 \
    ca-certificates \
    libopenmpi-dev \
    openmpi-bin \
    libfftw3-dev \
    libgomp1 && \
    # Clean up apt cache to reduce final image size
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Clone the LAMMPS source code from the official repository
# The 'stable' branch is used as it represents the latest stable release, suitable for production workloads
RUN git clone --branch stable https://github.com/lammps/lammps.git /usr/src/lammps

# Build LAMMPS with MPI support and the REAXFF package enabled
# This is a CPU-only build configured for performance (Release type)
RUN mkdir /usr/src/lammps/build && \
    cd /usr/src/lammps/build && \
    cmake ../cmake \
        -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
        -D BUILD_MPI=yes \
        -D PKG_REAXFF=yes && \
    # Compile using all available processor cores for a faster build
    make -j$(nproc) && \
    # Copy the main LAMMPS executable 'lmp' to a system location on the PATH
    # This makes the executable available globally without needing to modify PATH or use symlinks
    cp lmp /usr/local/bin/

# Set a working directory for application data and examples
WORKDIR /app

# Copy the specific ReaxFF example files for HNS into the working directory
# These files can be used for testing or as a starting point for simulations
RUN cp /usr/src/lammps/examples/reaxff/HNS/* .

# Clean up the downloaded source code to reduce the final image size
RUN rm -rf /usr/src/lammps

# Set a default command to provide an interactive shell
# In a Kubernetes deployment, this will typically be overridden by the pod's command/args
CMD ["/bin/bash"]

# MiniCluster manifest for a LAMMPS ReaxFF experiment on a single node.
# This configuration is designed for testing on a CPU-based Kubernetes cluster on AWS.
# API Version: Specifies the version of the Flux Operator CRD.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
# Kind: Defines the resource as a MiniCluster, managed by the Flux Operator.
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  # Name: A unique name for the MiniCluster instance.
  name: lammps-reaxff-hns-test
  # Namespace: The Kubernetes namespace where this MiniCluster will be deployed.
  namespace: default
spec:
  # Size: The number of pods in the MiniCluster. Set to 1 to run on a single node.
  size: 1
  # Tasks: The total number of MPI ranks or processes to run for the job.
  # The Flux Operator will translate this into `flux run -n <tasks> ...`
  tasks: 1
  # Cleanup: If false, the pods and their logs are retained after the job completes, which is useful for debugging.
  cleanup: false
  # Logging: Configures the logging behavior for the Flux Operator.
  logging:
    # Strict: When true, the operator will fail on any unknown logging keys.
    strict: true

  # Containers: Defines the container(s) that will run the user's application.
  containers:
    - # Image: The container image that contains the LAMMPS application and its dependencies.
      image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:lammps-reax
      # Command: The command to be executed by Flux. The operator will wrap this command with `flux run`.
      command: lmp -v x 2 -v y 2 -v z 2 -in ./in.reaxff.hns -nocite
      # Launcher: If false, this container is treated as a worker, and the job is launched by Flux itself.
      # If true, this container would be expected to launch the job (e.g., via flux submit).
      launcher: false

# MiniCluster manifest for a LAMMPS ReaxFF experiment on a single node.
# This configuration is a reset to a smaller scale for testing purposes,
# following a failure with a larger, node-specific configuration.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  # Name: A unique name for the MiniCluster instance.
  name: lammps-reaxff-hns-test
  # Namespace: The Kubernetes namespace where this MiniCluster will be deployed.
  namespace: default
spec:
  # Size: The number of pods in the MiniCluster. Set to 1 to run on a single node.
  size: 1
  # Tasks: The total number of MPI ranks. Updated to 8 to match the test command's decomposition (2*2*2).
  tasks: 8
  # Cleanup: If false, the pods and their logs are retained after the job completes, which is useful for debugging.
  cleanup: false
  # Logging: Configures the logging behavior for the Flux Operator.
  logging:
    # Strict: When true, the operator will fail on any unknown logging keys.
    strict: true

  # Containers: Defines the container(s) that will run the user's application.
  containers:
    - # Image: The container image that contains the LAMMPS application and its dependencies.
      image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:lammps-reax
      # Command: The command to be executed by Flux, reverted to a smaller scale for testing.
      command: lmp -v x 2 -v y 2 -v z 2 -in ./in.reaxff.hns -nocite
      # Launcher: If false, this container is treated as a worker, and the job is launched by Flux itself.
      launcher: false

updates.reason: Scaling up to the instance with the most cores (64-core hpc7g.16xlarge) to test application scalability. Matching MPI tasks to cores (64) and using a cubic domain decomposition (4x4x4) is a standard HPC optimization practice. Expecting a significant performance increase over the baseline.

The previous run on a 64-core ARM instance showed excellent performance (344.653 FOM). This attempt will test the best available x86 instance (48-core c7a.12xlarge) to compare if superior per-core performance can overcome the core count disadvantage. A near-cubic decomposition (4x4x3) will be used to optimize MPI communication for 48 tasks.

The 64-core ARM instance (hpc7g.16xlarge) achieved a FOM of 344.653, which is nearly 7x higher than the next best result on a 48-core x86 instance (51.430). The application scales well with core count, and we have tested the instance with the most available cores. Further attempts on instances with fewer cores are highly unlikely to surpass this peak performance. The optimization is complete.
